results.name: Grand Theft Auto VI Release Phishing Lures
results.description: Ahead of the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI release on November 19, 2026, threat actors are exploiting consumer hype through phishing campaigns and fraudulent schemes. Analysis of 121 newly registered domains containing 'cyberleek' and other GTA VI-themed domains revealed four primary lure categories: fake downloads impersonating popular leaker CyberLeek, false early access offers, nonexistent mobile versions, and free game promises. These malicious sites distribute trojans, request cryptocurrency payments, employ content lockers that require survey completion for affiliate revenue, and harvest personal information. Tactics include fake storefronts impersonating developer Rockstar, fraudulent APK files requiring unsafe installation permissions, and giveaway scams using urgency counters. Post-launch threats are expected to shift toward in-game currency fraud, credential phishing for Rockstar and gaming platform accounts, and malware distribution through fake cheats and modifications.

results.name: SkyW4lker Phishing Kit: Microsoft 365 Threat to US Firms
results.description: SkyW4lker is an active device-code phishing kit targeting Microsoft 365 users primarily in the United States, Europe, and other regions. By exploiting Microsoft's legitimate authentication process, attackers gain access to corporate accounts without stealing passwords or bypassing MFA. Between June and October 2026, 618 sandbox analyses identified related activity, with submissions increasing from 20 in June to 200 in September. The United States accounts for 47% of submissions, with organizations in technology, manufacturing, and government sectors most affected. The kit uses phishing emails with password-protected attachments containing links that lead victims through CAPTCHA pages to Microsoft's authentication system. Technical analysis reveals obfuscated JavaScript, IP-based geolocation, and polling mechanisms. SkyW4lker shares infrastructure and code modules with the Gabagool credential phishing kit, suggesting both were developed by the same actor.
targeted_countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

results.name: Binance heist: what we know, and what we see in TraderTraitor's toolkit
results.description: In October 2026, attackers stole approximately $6.34 billion from Binance in one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts on record. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation. The multi-stage compromise involved malicious software delivered through a fake job interview, where engineers were tricked into downloading trojanized developer tools including a weaponized Terraform provider. ReversingLabs analysis uncovered malicious components in their telemetry 77 days before public disclosure and identified backdoor variants with earlier submission histories. The attack chain progressed from initial developer workstation compromise through lateral movement to ultimately reach Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. The trojanized tools included FLATROOF and ROOFDECK backdoors hidden within legitimate-looking developer software, demonstrating sophisticated supply chain compromise techniques targeting DevOps environments.

results.name: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
results.description: Hackers potentially linked to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service exploited previously patched iOS and Android vulnerabilities to target visitors of multiple websites. The operation included impersonating america250.org, a site celebrating American independence, and a luxury UK hotel website near sensitive government institutions where Ukrainian President Zelenskyy stayed. Attackers used JavaScript injection, proxy domains, and compromised a Ukrainian web analytics service to deliver three different zero-click exploit chains, including the DarkSword iOS exploit kit. The attacks aimed to steal browser cookies, Wi-Fi passwords, and device data from diplomatic and high-profile targets related to Ukraine.
targeted_countries: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

results.name: Summary of Malicious Program Distribution via Goddess of Victory: NIKKE PC Launcher
results.description: Level Infinite disclosed that the PC launcher for the game "Goddess of Victory: NIKKE" was compromised when four script files on the official CDN were tampered with between September 27 and November 4, 2026. The modified scripts downloaded a remote access agent (internally named K2F) that could execute arbitrary commands, steal credentials from browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and cloud services. The malware persisted by injecting a DLL into Chrome and could intercept wallet recovery phrases. The compromise began with domain hijacking of insightjs.com on September 27, with script tampering occurring shortly after. Malicious payload distribution to users started October 30. Level Infinite detected the anomaly on November 4, replaced compromised files, and deployed automated detection and removal functionality on November 5. Users who launched the Windows PC launcher between September 27 and November 4 were potentially affected.

results.name: DarkBlinders: Active Espionage Campaign
results.description: A sophisticated cyberespionage operation targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq was conducted by DarkBlinders, the threat actor behind the Blinder Tunnel campaign. Active between August and October 2026, the campaign compromised a high-profile Israeli individual associated with the security sector and a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region. The operation employed government webmail, cloud-drive, and meeting-service lures, including phishing infrastructure impersonating the Gulf Cooperation Council Secretariat General and Kuwait's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. GitHub repositories under the PeakyBlindersTeam account served as command-and-control infrastructure. The attackers used selective activation, reviewing metadata from infected hosts before deploying a second-stage backdoor enabling PowerShell command execution. results.name: ClingSTUN Linux Backdoor Abuses Public STUN Infrastructure
results.description: A Linux malware strain named ClingSTUN exploits unpatched vulnerabilities in Internet-facing devices to establish persistent footholds and functions as a back-connect proxy backdoor. The campaign targets IoT devices through multiple CVEs including command injection and code execution flaws in various vendors' products. ClingSTUN abuses legitimate public STUN infrastructure to discover externally mapped IP addresses, maintain NAT bindings, and improve connectivity between compromised hosts and operators. The malware employs sophisticated persistence mechanisms, terminates watchdog timers, kills competitor processes, and disguises itself as the init process. It maintains remote command execution capabilities and includes self-propagation exploits for seven additional vulnerabilities. The threat actor evolved their approach across three distinct periods, adjusting initial access strategies and expanding the list of targeted vulnerabilities from single-vendor exploits to multi-vendor command injection attacks ...

results.name: ARTEX Exposed: Infrastructure Behind the South Korea Bank Hack
results.description: Between late September and early October 2026, seven South Korean financial institutions experienced breaches affecting approximately 66,000 individuals and 2,200 corporations. The intrusions were attributed to ARTEX, an AI-driven autonomous penetration testing framework. Investigation revealed exposed infrastructure at 38.244.50[.]120 and 23.248.226[.]250, uncovering AI model-routing components, custom Claude Code skills, proxy management utilities, and exploitation tooling. The operation utilized DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok models through the xcai[.]pro reseller domain. Recovered artifacts included FOFA reconnaissance tools, JNDI/LDAP exploitation chains, Linux privilege escalation exploits, cryptocurrency-exchange access scripts, and mobile-device utilities. The infrastructure spanned multiple countries with 1,303 distinct IP addresses identified through certificate, malware classification, and HTTP title hunting methods.

results.name: Not Actually Suspended: How a Bank-Phishing Network Fakes Its Own Takedown
results.description: A sophisticated phishing campaign targets 189 US financial institutions through 248 live look-alike domains using a distinctive naming pattern combining urgency keywords with bank names. The operation employs an innovative cloaking mechanism that displays fake "account suspended" pages to returning visitors while serving actual phishing content to first-time visitors, effectively evading takedown efforts. The infrastructure focuses on business banking and treasury portals, which provide access to larger balances and transfer capabilities. All domains operate behind Cloudflare, with hosting traced to shared servers at two providers. Network analysis reveals connections to a centralized backend managing additional phishing operations targeting UK, Netherlands, Australian, and New Zealand institutions. The campaign is administered through a jump server accessed via Remote Desktop from a UK residential broadband connection, representing the strongest lead to the operator's identity.

results.name: KeyHunter Operation: Harvard Alumni Data, Stanford Applications and LLM Key Theft
results.description: A Chinese-speaking threat actor identified as leepsmarts conducted a multi-vector operation combining LLM API credential theft with academic fraud targeting 20 universities. The campaign harvested 2,233 API keys from misconfigured cloud infrastructure across platforms like Vercel, Netlify, and Railway, with 12 marked valid. The actor created fraudulent student accounts at institutions including NYU, UC Berkeley, and Oregon State, while processing 195 Harvard alumni records from a torrent-distributed dataset. The operation employed AI agent frameworks through Telegram bots for automated scanning, validation, and account creation. Parallel financial fraud activities included a Harmony ONE cryptocurrency drainer capturing victim seed phrases and credit card validation using stolen Stripe merchant keys. Infrastructure spanning China, South Korea, Malaysia, and the US was discovered through an exposed directory listing revealing tools, scripts, and operational logs dating back to January 2026.
